title: The Rashbam: The Revolution of Peshat and the Shaping of Scholarly Exegesis in the Middle Ages
content:
The Rashbam: The Revolution of Peshat and the Shaping of Scholarly Exegesis in the Middle Ages
This article surveys the figure and the intellectual contribution of Rabbi Samuel ben Meir (the Rashbam), grandson of Rashi, who was among the pioneers of the peshat revolution in twelfth-century France. The text emphasizes the Rashbam's uncompromising commitment to analyzing "the deep plain meaning of Scripture," an approach that separates the linguistic-historical layer of the Torah from the accepted halakhic and homiletical interpretation. Beyond his revolutionary biblical commentaries, the source describes his central role as a leading Talmud commentator and one of the Tosafists, while examining his complex relations with his brother, Rabbenu Tam, and his response to the challenges of the Christian polemic. The aim of the text is to present the Rashbam as a bridging figure who combines scholarly integrity and exegetical innovation with deep loyalty to the tradition of Israel, leaving an eternal mark on the Jewish bookshelf.
The Work and Torah Thought of the Rashbam: The Revolution of Peshat and the Shaping of Scholarly Exegesis in the Middle Ages
The Historical and Genealogical Background of Rabbi Samuel ben Meir
Rabbi Samuel ben Meir, known by the acronym Rashbam, represents one of the most significant turning points in the history of Jewish exegesis in northern France in the twelfth century. Born around the year 1080 (4840 in the Hebrew calendar) and dying around 1160 (4920), the Rashbam was active at the very heart of early Ashkenazi Jewry, at a time when the educational and methodological institutions that would shape the Oral Torah and biblical exegesis for generations were beginning to take form.[1] As the eldest grandson of Rashi, the "Parshandata," the Rashbam not only inherited his grandfather's seat as a spiritual leader but also developed an independent, critical and daring exegetical consciousness, which set "the plain meaning of Scripture" as a supreme value standing on its own, at times even detached from the accepted halakhic tradition.[2, 3]
The life of the Rashbam is interwoven with the history of the Torah "royal family" of France. He was the son of Rabbi Meir ben Samuel and of Yocheved, Rashi's daughter, and the elder brother of the Rivam (Rabbi Isaac ben Meir) and of Rabbenu Tam (Rabbi Jacob ben Meir), the most dominant figure among the Tosafists.[1] This family setting was not merely a center of religious power but an intellectual laboratory in which questions of language, law and tradition were debated. The Rashbam merited to learn directly from his grandfather Rashi, and his testimony about the intellectual dialogue between them is a foundational document for understanding the development of peshat: he describes how he argued with his grandfather over the interpretation of Scripture, and how Rashi himself admitted that, had he had the leisure, he would have needed to write new commentaries based on "the plain meanings that are renewed every day."[2, 4]
The personal bond between the Rashbam and Rashi was not only that of disciple and teacher but a partnership in building a new storey in the edifice of the Torah. The Rashbam saw himself as the one who brings from potential into actuality his grandfather's late aspiration, to cleanse biblical commentary of midrashic influences that do not accord with the language of the text and with its logical and literary context.[5] His work took place against the background of a stormy period that included the First Crusade, growing tensions with the Christian Church, and an intellectual flowering that sought to anchor Judaism in firm foundations of reason and language.[2, 6]
The Deep Plain Meaning of Scripture: The Exegetical Methodology
The Rashbam's exegetical thought rests on the sharp and uncompromising distinction between "peshat" (the plain meaning) and "derash" (homiletical interpretation). Whereas Rashi aspired to present the peshat but incorporated into it many midrashim of the Sages in order to resolve difficulties in the text, the Rashbam argued that the biblical text has an independent existence on the literal and rational level, which is not necessarily subordinate to halakhic or aggadic midrash.[4, 5] He coined the term "the deep plain meaning of Scripture," which expresses the aspiration to penetrate through the later layers of interpretation and arrive at the original intention of the text as it emerges from its immediate context, from the rules of grammar and from human reason.[3, 5]
The Rashbam does not deny the authority of the Sages or the necessity of derash for the observance of the commandments. On the contrary, he emphasizes that derash is "the essence of the Torah" from a practical standpoint, but he argues that the Torah was written in the language of human beings and therefore has "seventy faces" that do not contradict one another but operate on different planes.[4, 7] His approach is phenomenological: he seeks to understand how the text works, what its linguistic conventions are, and how ideas develop across the weekly portions.[5]
One of the Rashbam's central contributions is the understanding that Scripture uses literary techniques to convey messages. He points to linguistic duplications, to chiastic structures, and to the use of leitwörter (guiding words) as tools for understanding the text.[5] For example, in his commentary on Jacob's blessing of his sons in Parashat Vayechi, he criticizes Rashi for having interpreted the blessing of Dan as a prophecy about Samson. In his view, "whoever interprets it as referring to Samson did not know the deep plain meaning of Scripture," since it is implausible that Jacob would prophesy about a single individual who would appear hundreds of years later in a specific situation; rather, the peshat requires that the blessing deal with the general character of the tribe of Dan as "the rearguard of all the camps" in Israel's wars.[5] Here the Rashbam is revealed as a historical-literary commentator who seeks to see the overall picture and not only the local homily.
The Tension between Peshat and Halakha: The Case of "And There Was Evening and There Was Morning"
The most revolutionary and daring aspect of the Rashbam's exegesis is his readiness to propose interpretations that stand in direct contradiction to the established halakha, so long as they follow necessarily from the peshat. The most famous case is his interpretation of the verse "And there was evening and there was morning, one day" in the Creation story.[2, 8] Whereas halakha determines categorically that the day begins in the evening (and therefore the Sabbath and the festivals begin at sunset), the Rashbam argues that according to the peshat the day ended only on the morning of the following day.[8]
According to his explanation, the expression "and there was evening" means that the day ended and the light set, and "and there was morning" means that the night passed and dawn rose, and only then was "one day" complete.[8] This interpretation does not aim to change the time at which the Sabbath enters in practice, since the Rashbam is committed to the tradition of the Sages, but seeks to clarify the original order of Creation as it is described in the text.[2] This approach aroused sharp opposition, particularly from Rabbi Abraham ibn Ezra, who in his "Epistle of the Sabbath" came out against such interpretations that might undermine the faith of the masses in the observance of the Sabbath.[2] But for the Rashbam, the scholarly truth of the peshat is an independent religious value that cannot be subordinated to apologetic or halakhic needs.[7]
This separation between the world of interpretation and the world of practice is also expressed in the commandment of tefillin. On the verse "And you shall bind them as a sign upon your hand," the Rashbam proposes that on the level of peshat it is a metaphor for constant remembrance, similar to verses in Song of Songs and Proverbs that call on a person to bind words of ethical instruction upon his heart.[7] Nevertheless, he does not exempt a person from putting on physical tefillin, but argues that the commandment as it is actually performed is the fruit of derash and received tradition, whereas the written verse seeks to emphasize the spiritual dimension of remembrance.[7] This distinction enables the Rashbam to preserve intellectual integrity as a commentator without harming his loyalty as a Jew who observes the commandments.
Another example of preferring realistic logic over the accepted midrashic interpretation is found in the passage on paid guardians. On the verse "If it be torn in pieces, let him bring it as evidence," Rashi explains that the guardian must bring witnesses to the court.[5] The Rashbam argues that this interpretation is not acceptable, since shepherds are in a remote field and it is implausible that witnesses would be there.[5] He therefore explains that "evidence" here means physical proof: the guardian must bring the remains of the animal (an ear, the legs), as described in the book of Amos, to prove that it was torn by a beast and not stolen.[5] This is a realistic interpretation based on an understanding of the conditions of life in the ancient East, and on a deep affinity between the books of the Torah and the Prophets.[5]
The Rashbam as Talmud Commentator and Tosafist
Despite his fame as a biblical commentator, the Rashbam was first and foremost a man of halakha and Talmud, one of the earliest and most important of the Tosafists.[3] His work in this field is characterized by a combination of Rashi's precise, local commentary with the broad, dialectical method of give-and-take of the Tosafot.[3] His greatest contribution is the completion of the commentary on tractates in which Rashi did not manage to complete his work or in which his commentary was lost.
The most prominent example is tractate Bava Batra. Rashi's commentary on this tractate breaks off at folio 29a, in the chapter "Chezkat HaBatim," and his place is taken by the Rashbam's commentary, which serves as the basic commentary in all editions of the Talmud to the end of the tractate.[3] This commentary is considered far longer and more comprehensive than Rashi's; whereas Rashi tends toward brilliant concision, the Rashbam elaborates on every step of the discussion, presents the difficulties and their answers in full, and often sums up the halakha for practice at the end of the discussion.[3] This tendency toward length derives from the Rashbam's pedagogical outlook, as he sought to create a commentary that would allow the student to understand the discussion without the need for external aids.[3]
In the chapter "Arvei Pesachim" (the last chapter of tractate Pesachim), Rashi's and the Rashbam's commentaries appear side by side.[3] When the later Tosafists cite the "Kuntres" (a designation usually reserved for Rashi) in tractate Bava Batra or in the tenth chapter of Pesachim, they actually mean the Rashbam, which attests to the immense authority he attained as the principal commentator on the Talmud in these tractates.[3]
The Rashbam wrote commentaries on many other tractates, such as Eruvin, Gittin, Bava Kamma, Pirkei Avot, Chullin and Niddah, but unfortunately most of them did not survive as independent works.[3, 5] However, his novellae were absorbed into the words of the Tosafists and are cited thousands of times in the Talmud. The Rashbam is considered to have laid the foundations of the Western method of pilpul (dialectical analysis), but he always insisted that the talmudic discussion be anchored in the "peshat of the sugya" (the plain sense of the talmudic passage), exactly as he insisted on the peshat of Scripture.[3] His work on the Talmud constitutes an essential link: on the one hand it continues the exegetical tradition of his family, and on the other it breaks a path toward the conceptual and comparative analysis that would characterize the later generations of the Tosafists.[3, 11]
Halakhic Disputes within the Family: The Rashbam and Rabbenu Tam
The relationship between the Rashbam and his younger brother Rabbenu Tam is one of the fascinating chapters in the history of Torah study. Although the Rashbam was the elder brother and even served as Rabbenu Tam's teacher, the two disagreed on dozens of halakhic and exegetical issues.[12, 13] Their disagreements often reflect the tension between loyalty to the tradition of Rashi (which the Rashbam led) and the innovative, challenging and dialectical approach of Rabbenu Tam.
The most famous dispute concerns the order of the passages in tefillin.[13, 14] The Rashbam held to the view of his grandfather Rashi, according to which the order of the passages in the compartments should follow the order of their appearance in the Torah ("the passages in their order"). Rabbenu Tam, on the basis of an analysis of the words of the Gemara in Menachot and other sources, innovated a different order in which "the Vav-Heh passages are in the middle" (the passages "And it shall be, if you shall hearken" and "Hear" are interchanged).[13, 14, 15] This dispute is not merely technical; it touches on questions of authority, the interpretation of sources, and ancestral tradition. Although the ruling of the Shulchan Arukh follows the opinion of Rashi and the Rashbam, the Jewish custom of also putting on the tefillin of Rabbenu Tam as a stringency stems from the immense respect felt for the sages of Ramerupt.[13, 16]
Another dispute concerns the laws of the Sabbath, regarding pouring from a first vessel onto spices.[12] The Rashbam sometimes permitted such pouring in certain cases, whereas Rabbenu Tam forbade it entirely on account of "cooking."[12] Here too the Rashbam leans toward the linguistic and realistic interpretation of the words of the Sages, while Rabbenu Tam applies a system of objections and logical inferences that make the law stricter.
The Rashbam and Rabbenu Tam represent two models of scholarship: the Rashbam is the "Sinai," the master of tradition and of command of the peshat, whereas Rabbenu Tam is the "uprooter of mountains," the dialectician who seeks to create harmony between contradictory passages throughout the Talmud.[3] The disputes between them do not attest to a rift but to a family and intellectual dynamic that fertilized the world of Torah in France and enabled the Tosafot method to flourish in its full splendor.
Religious Polemic and the Use of Philological Tools
The Rashbam's work was not done in a vacuum but within a Christian environment that posed difficult exegetical and theological challenges. The twelfth century was a period of flowering in Christian exegesis, and the Church began to use arguments based on the (allegorical) analysis of verses in order to prove the truth of Christianity.[2, 6] The Rashbam was among the first of the sages of France to integrate into his commentaries direct polemic against Christian interpretation and against the Latin Vulgate translation.[2, 5]
His use of "peshat" served as a defensive weapon: by demonstrating the literal and contextual meaning of the text, he negated the Christian interpretations that saw in the Hebrew Bible metrological hints of Jesus.[5] For example, with regard to messianic verses or the vessels of the Temple, the Rashbam took care to explain them in their historical and physical context, thereby rejecting the Christian attempt to turn every detail in Scripture into an ecclesiastical spiritual symbol.[2, 6] He even pointed out linguistic errors in the Latin translation, which attests to a certain acquaintance with foreign languages and to great self-confidence in his knowledge of the Hebrew language.[5]
The Rashbam's linguistic knowledge was greatly influenced by the grammarians of Spain, such as Menachem ben Saruq and Dunash ben Labrat, whose books reached France ("Ispamia").[3, 5] He himself composed a book of grammar called "Dikdukot of Rabbenu Samuel," in which he dealt with the rules of the language, vocalization and cantillation marks.[3] For the Rashbam, grammar is not an ancillary discipline but an indispensable tool for understanding the Torah; without precision regarding the structure of the verb or the preposition, one cannot arrive at "the deep plain meaning of Scripture."[3]
In addition, the Rashbam showed great interest in the sciences and in natural phenomena. In his commentaries one finds references to the structure of the world, to biological processes, and to the customs of other peoples, all with the aim of making Scripture an understandable and living book.[3] This approach, which combines immense Torah erudition with openness to the outside world, made his commentary one of the important sources for understanding the world of medieval Jews.
The Fate of the Commentaries and the Lost Manuscripts
Despite its decisive importance, the Rashbam's commentary on the Torah did not enjoy wide circulation like Rashi's commentary and remained largely the possession of a few learners and of the sages of France alone.[3] Some wonder why so brilliant a work did not become popular; perhaps the reason lies in its research-oriented and lengthy character, or perhaps in its sharp clash with halakha in several places, which aroused apprehension among copyists.[2] Whereas Rashi provided a commentary suited to every age and every level, the Rashbam wrote a commentary for the educated and the scholars who seek to investigate the roots of things.[2]
Most of the Rashbam's commentaries on the other books of the Hebrew Bible were lost over the generations.[3] His commentary on the Torah survived in a single manuscript found in Breslau (Wrocław), Poland, but tragically the manuscript was lost during the Holocaust.[3] Fortunately, David Rosin managed to publish a scholarly edition of the manuscript in 1882, and on its basis we study the commentary today.[3] In recent decades additional remnants and commentaries attributed to the Rashbam have been discovered in other manuscripts, such as his commentary on Job, Ecclesiastes, Song of Songs and parts of Psalms.[3]
The Rashbam's commentaries on the Five Megillot are characterized by the same loyalty to peshat, but they also include impressive literary analysis. In his commentary on Song of Songs, for example, he addresses the question of the allegory and its referent; he is not content with the general statement that it concerns the love of God and Israel, but analyzes the human love described in the verses in its own right, with the understanding that the spiritual referent can rest only on a stable and comprehensible allegory.[17] In this he anticipated modern literary study of the Bible by hundreds of years.
Summary and Conclusions: The Rashbam as a Shaper of Consciousness
Rabbi Samuel ben Meir stands in the annals of history as a figure of "an innovator within the tradition." He did not seek to shatter the world of halakha that his grandfather Rashi labored so hard to build, but sought to add to it a storey of intellectual clarity and scholarly integrity.[3, 4] His work spans the entire Torah: from Hebrew grammar to talmudic pilpul, from the defense of the faith against Christianity to a daring investigation of the order of Creation.[2, 3, 5]
His principal contribution is the transformation of peshat into a critical and creative tool. He taught his generation and the generations after it that the biblical text can be understood with human, linguistic and logical tools, without this harming its sanctity.[7] His disputes with Rabbenu Tam underscore the vitality of the beit midrash in France, a place where truth was investigated without fear, even when it led to conclusions different from the accepted ones.[13]
The fact that his commentaries on the Talmud (Bava Batra and Pesachim) are printed at the heart of the Talmud to this day ensures that the voice of the Rashbam will continue to be heard in every yeshiva and in every Jewish bookshelf.[3] He remains a symbol of the scholar who combines depth with simplicity, family tradition with personal independence, and love of Torah with the pursuit of truth. His thought, based on "the plain meanings that are renewed every day," invites every learner in every generation to continue to discover new layers within the eternal text of the people of Israel.[4]
